newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian pepper prices red-hot on supply woes.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian pepper prices red-hot on supply woes.

text.p: Indonesian pepper is hot on international markets, with local prices at an eight-year high due to a drop in production, industry sources said on Thursday.
They said the prices had more than doubled since January. The Jakarta-based International Pepper Community (IPC) said prices were expected to be firm through 1997.
"There has been a drastic shortfall in Indonesian production because of bad weather and the incidence of pests," IPC economist K.C. Ponnana told Reuters in an interview.
The IPC is an inter-governmental body that links seven major producers -- led by India and Indonesia -- who account for around 95 percent of global pepper production.
Ponnana said Indonesia's pepper production had been revised down to 38,000 tonnes this year from an earlier forecast of 46,440 tonnes, compared with 39,200 tonnes in 1996.

Indonesian traders said pepper was quoted at 7,200 rupiah ($2.95) per kg on Thursday, compared with a mere 2,650 rupiah ($1.09) in January -- an increase of more that 170 percent. They said local prices hit a high of 8,000 rupiah in 1989.
The export price had climbed more than 40 percent to $3,850 per tonne from $2,700 in the same period.
The world's top consumers of pepper, the mostly widely used spice, are in North America, the European Union, the Middle East and North Africa.
The traders said Indonesia's pepper harvest was expected to begin in July and stretch through September, but added that the outlook on production was dim.
"My estimate is that we will see a decline of 30 percent from last year," one trader from the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra said.
"Prices are excellent, but growers have much less to sell now," he said. "Carry-over stocks are below 2,000 tonnes because players have been selling to cash in on the good prices."
The trader said he expected prices to hold their ground the rest of this year because of good demand and tight supply.

The IPC's Ponnana said the combined production of the IPC's six leading members -- India, Indonesia, Brazil, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka -- was forecast at 146,563 tonnes in 1997, down from 147,785 tonnes last year and 161,674 in 1995.
The IPC estimated 1997 production in non-member Vietnam at 20,000 tonnes, unchanged over the last three years, and China's output declining to 10,000 tonnes from 11,754 tonnes in 1996.

An IPC official said attempts were being made to bring Vietnam into the grouping. Similar attempts are being made by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) because Vietnam is Asia's largest coffee producer after Indonesia.

"The prospects for pepper this year are bright, with prices rising significantly from January to May this year," Ponnana said. "With purchasing power increasing in Asia and elsewhere, we will see increased consumption of pepper."

"We can already see the trend from the mushrooming of restaurants and fast-food chains in cities around Asia," he said. "They are particularly visible in urban and semi-urban centres where the purchasing power is increasing."
